verdicts.rewritten_summary: National-framework source (applies country-wide, including the state of Malacca): the Human Dignity Trust Malaysia country profile (last updated 2024) reports the Federal Penal Code 1936 ss.377A/377B criminalise same-sex sexual activity with a maximum penalty of twenty years’ imprisonment and whipping, and s.377D “outrages on decency” criminalises gross indecency in terms that can be used to target transgender people; state Sharia enactments additionally criminalise “cross-dressing” for Muslims. It records evidence of the law being enforced in recent years, a crackdown on the LGBT community since the 2018 election, a high-profile 2021 case of a prominent transgender woman fleeing the country following threats of arrest, and consistent reports of discrimination and violence with transgender people particularly vulnerable to physical and verbal abuse.

National-framework source (applies country-wide; no Malacca-specific breakdown): HRW report (published 10 Aug 2022 with Justice for Sisters) documents government-sponsored discrimination against LGBT people in Malaysia, citing the federal penal code punishing oral and anal sex with up to 20 years in prison and Sharia law codes in the federal territories of Kuala Lumpur and Putrajaya that typically criminalise same-sex activity and gender nonconformity. It details a hostile official climate — “rehabilitation” and conversion programs, officials shutting down events, and the 2021 prosecution of transgender woman Nur Sajat in western Selangor — and concludes pervasive antipathy toward sexual and gender diversity influences law enforcement, judicial outcomes, family behavior, and public discourse.

Region-specific: BBC News (article dated 9 Aug 2024) reports the beaten, bruised body of 33-year-old transgender TikToker “Abuja Area Mama” was found along the Katampe-Mabushi expressway in the Banex/Wuse II area of Abuja on Thursday 8 August 2024, hours after she posted a final video, having previously expressed fear for her life; a police statement described the victim as “a man fully dressed in female clothing with no means of identification”. Abuja police chief Benneth Igweh ordered a “thorough and discreet” investigation, and the article notes that although Nigerian laws guarantee freedom from discrimination, mass arrests and detention of LGBTQ+ people are common, especially in northern states.

Region-specific: The Dial (Issue 25) reports police found Area Mama dead on an Abuja highway hours after her last video; Abuja police’s preliminary statement described her as “a man fully dressed in female clothing”, and six months later no suspects had been charged despite a promised “thorough and discreet” investigation. It details the legal floor her killers faced — the Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 reinforcing colonial-era laws criminalising same-sex activity as “carnal knowledge against the order of nature” punishable by up to 14 years’ imprisonment, bans on same-sex marriage and civil unions, gay organisations and public LGBTQ+ expression, death-by-stoning risk under northern Sharia law, no legal route to change gender, and cross-dressing bans under Sharia in the north and in the Nigerian military — and records a nearly 6,000-signature petition demanding investigation of her murder as a hate crime.

National-framework source (applies country-wide; no Abuja-specific breakdown): Sahara Reporters (19 Aug 2026) reports the United Kingdom's foreign office warned LGBT+ travellers to Nigeria of the risk of arrest, violence, attacks, blackmail and intimidation. The advisory states same-sex sexual activity is illegal and can attract lengthy prison sentences, that some northern states operating under Sharia law can impose the death penalty, and that the law also extends to people who help arrange or conduct same-sex marriages and criminalises activities involving gay groups and organisations; breaching curfews or movement restrictions could expose travellers to arrest and detention.

National-framework source (binds Lima as national policy): Infobae (20 Feb 2025) reports the Congress Women and Family Commission unanimously approved the Muñante initiative barring trans people from public bathrooms of the sex not matching their biological sex at birth, stating the text also bars “ambiguous” bathroom signage of the kind the international airport Jorge Chávez had placed (“for all persons with female identity” / “male identity”) and that the norm still required plenary backing. LGBTIQ activist Gianna Camacho is quoted calling the measure discriminatory and describing how enforcement would reduce to security staff demanding ID (DNI) based on their own judgment of whether a woman entering is trans.

National-framework source (the norm is national policy, enacted by the congress that sits and operates in Lima): IDEHPUCP analysis (15 Apr 2025, Miriam Tovar and Gonzalo Ugarte) reports the Congress plenary on Wednesday 2 April 2025 approved, exempt from a second vote, the fused bills 6505/2023-CR and 8457/2023-CR; article 5 of the text prohibits entry to and use of public sanitary facilities by any person whose biological sex does not match the sex for which the facility is designated, with listed exceptions. The authors call the rule direct legislation that conditions basic rights on a “biological sex”, a violation of the equality and non-discrimination principle, and note trans people, though framed as aggressors, are more often victims of violence and discrimination.

National-framework source (observatory counts include Lima): Agencia Presentes (22 Jul 2024) reports the TLGBI Rights Observatory annual report recorded 54 murders of TLGBI people and 170 reports of rights violations between 2020 and 2023, more than half of the dead being trans women (30), followed by 23 gay men and one lesbian; 2023 saw the most homicides (19) and no suspects were identified in 26 of the 54 killings. It recounts the 12 Feb 2023 kidnapping of transgender sex worker Rubí Torres Silvano (31) from jirón Chancay in central Lima by the “Los Gallegos” extortion gang, who killed her with roughly 30 gunshots, and flags state inaction: no official system records victims’ sexual orientation and hate crimes go unsanctioned.

Source for this record (national norm + Lima-city detail): Infobae (20 Feb 2025) reports the Congress Women and Family Commission unanimously approved the bill barring trans people from public bathrooms of the sex not matching their biological sex at birth; the text also obliges removal of “ambiguous” signage of the kind the international airport Jorge Chávez had placed (“for all persons with female identity” / “male identity”). Activist Gianna Camacho is quoted warning enforcement will amount to ID (DNI) checks by security staff judging who may enter a bathroom, which she calls discriminatory and based on prejudice.

Source for this record (capital-scene violence data): Agencia Presentes (22 Jul 2024) reports the Observatory recorded 54 murders of TLGBI people and 170 reported rights violations in Peru 2020–2023, trans women the most affected (30 of 54 dead), 19 homicides in 2023, and no identified suspects in 26 killings. It names the 12 Feb 2023 “Los Gallegos” gang kidnapping of trans sex worker Rubí Torres Silvano (31) from jirón Chancay in central Lima, killed with roughly 30 gunshots, as an example of the capital pattern, and notes the state keeps no system recording sexual orientation in killings.

National-framework source (applies country-wide; the package is drafted and enforced by institutions operating in Ankara): HRW (29 Oct 2025) reports the leaked draft “11th Judicial Package” would amend the Turkish penal code to criminalise conduct deemed contrary to biological sex and general morality with up to three years’ prison, participation in same-sex engagement or marriage ceremonies with up to four years, and would raise the minimum age for gender-affirming care including surgery from 18 to 25 with mandatory permanent infertility and repeated evaluations at government-approved hospitals; healthcare professionals performing such interventions would face fines and up to seven years in prison, trans people receiving deemed-illegal care up to three years, and courts could order pretrial detention. Fifteen LGBT groups and the Turkish Medical Association opposed the draft.

National-framework monitoring report (the institutions it names — the presidency, the Ministry of Family — operate in Ankara): Kaos GL’s annual report (“The Year of the Family: A Major Siege Against LGBTI+ People”, launched in 2025) finds LGBTI+ hostility became explicit state policy — hostility centered on the presidency, the Ministry of Family as implementing ministry, broadcasts censored and artistic events cancelled or banned, and an LGBTI+ association closed for the first time in years with criminal cases opened against 11 of its members. It documents six violations of the right to life (three recorded as hate-motivated), trans people the most affected, a sharp rise in torture and ill-treatment violations (89 versus 51 the previous year), and notes the state keeps no official hate-crime statistics.

National-framework source (applies country-wide; no Eskişehir-specific breakdown): HRW (29 Oct 2025) reports the leaked “11th Judicial Package” draft would criminalise conduct deemed contrary to biological sex and general morality with up to three years’ prison, participation in same-sex engagement or marriage ceremonies with up to four years, and would raise the minimum age for gender-affirming care from 18 to 25 with mandatory permanent infertility and repeated evaluations at government-approved hospitals; providers could face fines and up to seven years in prison and patients up to three years, with pretrial detention possible. Fifteen LGBT groups and the Turkish Medical Association opposed the draft.

National-framework source (applies country-wide; no Gaziantep-specific breakdown): HRW (29 Oct 2025) reports the leaked “11th Judicial Package” draft would criminalise conduct deemed contrary to biological sex and general morality with up to three years’ prison, same-sex ceremony participation with up to four years, and would raise the minimum age for gender-affirming care from 18 to 25 with mandatory permanent infertility and repeated evaluations at government-approved hospitals; providers could face fines and up to seven years in prison and patients up to three years, with pretrial detention possible. Fifteen LGBT groups and the Turkish Medical Association opposed the draft.

verdicts.note: rule-5 tie-break drop: record text makes no claim this parent-country framework doc supports (its facts are Istanbul-specific and covered by the region's own sources); fact belongs on the parent TUR record

verdicts.rewritten_summary: Source covering this record’s claims: Kaos GL’s 2025 annual report (“The Year of the Family: A Major Siege Against LGBTI+ People”) documents state-policy hostility country-wide including Istanbul specifically — “especially in Istanbul, intensified practices of sealing or closing homes” obstructing access to housing. Its monitoring also records six violations of the right to life (three recorded as hate-motivated), trans people the most affected, torture and ill-treatment violations nearly doubled (89, up from 51), an LGBTI+ association closed with criminal cases against 11 members, and the state keeping no official hate-crime statistics.
